source_refs.note: g) Identification of Zinc radical (Zn²⁺): a main subheading of 16.7 Tests for identification of basic radicals, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 347-348.

blocks.text: Take 4 g solid sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ of distilled water. Make two portions of the above solution for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of zinc radical
rows: To one portion add NaOH solution.
White precipitate is formed which is soluble in excess of NaOH solution.
To second portion of the above solution add aqueous ammonia.
White precipitate is formed which dissolves in excess of ammonia.

blocks.prompt: a) What is lake test? Give equation.
blocks.explanation:
It is the test for Al³⁺. A little NaOH (or ammonia) is added to the Al³⁺ solution to precipitate Al(OH)₃, and blue litmus solution is added. The gelatinous Al(OH)₃ adsorbs the dye on its surface and a blue layer (a ‘blue lake’) forms:
Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃, then Al(OH)₃ + litmus → blue lake

blocks.prompt: b) How ammonium ion is indicated?
blocks.explanation: Warm the sample gently with NaOH solution. Ammonia gas with its characteristic smell is given off, and it turns moist red litmus blue: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O

blocks.prompt: c) How will you distinguish ferrous (Fe²⁺) and ferric (Fe³⁺) radicals?
blocks.explanation: With NaOH, Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate of Fe(OH)₂ that turns orange-brown after some time, whereas Fe³⁺ at once gives an orange-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃.

rows: green precipitate of Fe(OH)₂ with NaOH
orange-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃ with NaOH

blocks.prompt: d) What happens when aq. NH₃ is added to Cu²⁺ solution in limited and excess quantities?
blocks.explanation: With a little ammonia a pale blue precipitate (Cu(OH)₂, or [Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂]) forms. With excess ammonia the precipitate dissolves, giving a deep blue solution of the complex ion [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.
